lines.text: A land of valley kingdoms beneath the highest mountains on Earth. This is the story of Nepal, from the birth of the Buddha to a republic shaped by its young.
It begins in the foothills of the south, at Lumbini, where by tradition a prince was born who would become the Buddha, and found one of the great faiths.
In the Kathmandu Valley, the Licchavi kings left the oldest written records of Nepal, and grew rich on trade between India and Tibet.
Then came the Mallas, who split the valley into the rival cities of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur, and filled their squares with temples.
One Newar artist of the valley, Araniko, carried its skill to Tibet and on to Kublai Khan's court, where he built the White Stupa in Beijing.
Far to the west, in the hill kingdom of Gorkha, a new royal house took power: the Shahs, who would one day rule all of Nepal.
Their great king was Prithvi Narayan Shah, who joined dozens of small hill states and set his sights on the rich valley.
In 1768 he conquered Kathmandu, and the kingdom of Nepal was born, a Himalayan country that holds eight of the world's highest peaks.
In the new kingdom, the poet Bhanubhakta Acharya retold the Ramayana in plain Nepali verse, and became the first great poet of the language.
But Nepal's expansion met the British East India Company. In two years of war, it lost about a third of its land.
The Treaty of Sugauli ended the fighting and drew most of the borders Nepal has today. Gurkha soldiers began to serve the British.
In 1846, after a massacre at court, the general Jung Bahadur Rana seized power and made the office of prime minister his family's by right.
For a century the Ranas ruled while the kings reigned only in name, and Nepal was kept closed to the outside world.
It was a king who broke them. In 1950 Tribhuvan fled to the Indian embassy, and returned the next year to restore royal rule and promise democracy.
Meanwhile, the poet Laxmi Prasad Devkota, called the Great Poet, wrote the beloved love poem Muna Madan.
From the Sherpa country came Tenzing Norgay, a mountaineer who would one day stand on top of the world.
B. P. Koirala, of the Nepali Congress, would become the first elected prime minister of Nepal, and spend long years in prison and exile for it.
His comrade Ganesh Man Singh fought Rana rule, and decades later led the movement that brought back multi-party democracy.
From New Zealand came Edmund Hillary, who would climb Everest with Tenzing and spend his life building schools and hospitals for the Sherpas.
Mahendra, Tribhuvan's son, would take the throne and dismiss the elected government, ruling through the partyless Panchayat system.
In 1934 a great earthquake struck, killing more than ten thousand people and flattening much of the old towns of the valley.
In Japan, Junko Tabei was born. She would become the first woman to reach the summit of Everest.
Birendra, the next king, would accept a multi-party constitution after the protests of 1990, before a terrible night in 2001.
His brother Gyanendra would come to the throne after that night, and be the last king of Nepal.
In 1950 the Nepali Congress rose in arms, backed by the king and by India. Within months, a century of Rana rule was over and Nepal opened its doors.
Sushila Karki would become Nepal's first woman chief justice, and much later, its first woman prime minister.
On the twenty-ninth of May 1953, Hillary and Tenzing stood on the summit of Everest, the first to be confirmed at the top of the world.
Pushpa Kamal Dahal, known as Prachanda, would lead a Maoist insurgency, and then the first government of the republic.
Bidya Devi Bhandari would become the first woman president of Nepal.
And Pasang Lhamu Sherpa would be the first Nepali woman to reach the top of Everest, in 1993, though she died on the way down.
In the lowland jungle of the Terai, Chitwan became Nepal's first national park, a refuge for tigers and for the one-horned rhino, which has since recovered.
Three years later, the land around Everest itself was protected, home of the Sherpa people, the snow leopard and the red panda.
Balen Shah, an engineer and rapper, would become mayor of Kathmandu, and after the protests of 2025, prime minister.
In 1996 the Maoists took up arms against the monarchy. Ten years of civil war followed, and more than seventeen thousand people died.
That same year, a sudden storm caught climbers high on Everest, and eight died in a single day.
In 2001, at a palace dinner, King Birendra, the queen and seven of their family were shot dead. An inquiry blamed the crown prince.
When King Gyanendra seized full power, weeks of strikes and protests forced him to recall parliament, and the monarchy soon came to an end.
In 2015, an earthquake centred in Gorkha killed nearly nine thousand people, toppled old temples and set off a deadly avalanche on Everest.
That same year, an elected assembly gave Nepal a new constitution, as a secular federal republic of seven provinces.
In 2025, young people rose against corruption and a ban on social media. Parliament burned, the prime minister resigned, and a new chapter began.
From the Buddha's birthplace to a young republic, Nepal's story is still being written beneath its mountains.
